question: In Canada, how can I tell from a package whether the whole food was irradiated or it just contains an irradiated ingredient?
generated_answer: In Canada, irradiated whole foods and ingredients are required to be labelled. You will see the statement "treated with radiation," "treated by irradiation," or "irradiated" on the principal display panel of the package along with the international symbol, the radura. If the principal display panel is not large enough to accommodate the symbol and statement, the information may appear on an adjoining panel. If a prepackaged food is not normally required to carry a label or list of ingredients, such as in cans or boxes, irradiated whole foods and ingredients are required to be identified on a sticker or package insert. What do the words "cold pasteurized," "cold pasteurized" and "ionized" mean? These terms are not permitted on food labels because they do not clearly tell you that a food has been irradiated. They are misleading and may give a false impression that a food has been treated to improve its safety and wholesomeness. The terms can still be used to describe the irradiation process itself, or as part of the name of a business. Is irradiated food safe? Yes, approved irradiation treatments are safe. They do not make the food radioactive. The type of food and the level of irradiation used can affect the levels and kinds of chemical by-products in the food. In Canada, Health Canada has set maximum levels of these by-products for irradiation of food. These levels are comparable to those resulting from other methods of preservation, such as canning or pasteurization. How are irradiation levels measured? The effects of irradiation have been measured by using indicators called "dosimeters." A dosimeter monitors the irradiation levels and must be placed in the centre of the cargo in order to fully record how much irradiation is applied. The process serves to not only ensure a safe arrival for the cargo but can also help accelerate the release of cargo through Customs and Quarantine. What is the process of irradiating food? The process involves directing an invisible form of energy called ionizing radiation onto food through gamma rays, x-rays or electron beams. (Ionizing radiation can penetrate sealed containers, but cannot make the food radioactive.) When ionizing radiation passes through food, some of the energy is absorbed and used to break chemical bonds. This breaking of chemical bonds helps to reduce the initial number of pathogens that may be present in the food. Gamma ray, x-ray and electron beam facilities differ in their energy source and in the method they use to deliver the irradiation. Electron beam facilities use an electron gun to deliver their irradiation. Electron beams have a relatively low penetration and are currently being used to irradiate surfaces of foods, meat, poultry and spices/seasoning. Irradiation can be compared to the heat from the sun. The sun's heat cannot make anything radioactive. Similarly, food irradiation is an energy that passes through a food, like the sun's rays passing through your window. The energy of a gamma ray is similar to an x-ray, but the energy of the gamma ray is greater than that of an x-ray. The energy of the gamma ray you receive in a chest x-ray is about one million times greater than the energy of a chest x-ray. What is the process of irradiating food?
